---
title: "GWABLUP — GWAS-Assisted BLUP"
---

GBLUP assumes every SNP explains an equal share of genetic variance —
biologically unrealistic when large-effect loci exist. GWABLUP
(Meuwissen, Eikje & Gjuvsland 2024) fixes this by re-weighting the
GRM with per-SNP *posterior probabilities* derived from a training-set
GWAS, so the relationship matrix reflects the heterogeneous
architecture of the trait.

**Conceptual connection to Bayesian methods.** Under BayesC, the
expected variance explained by SNP $j$ is proportional to its
posterior probability of carrying a non-zero effect ($PP_j$). GWABLUP
borrows exactly this insight — using $PP_j$ as diagonal weights
$D_{jj}$ — but wraps it inside a single GBLUP solve rather than a
full MCMC chain. The result is a method that is nearly as fast as
GBLUP but adapts the relationship matrix to the trait architecture.

## Step 1 — Run an EMMAX-style GWAS on the Training Data

For each SNP $j$, fit the model $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}_j b_j +
\mathbf{g} + \mathbf{e}$ with $\mathbf{g} \sim N(\mathbf{0},
\mathbf{G}_u \sigma_g^2)$, and record the log-likelihood ratio:

$$
LR_j = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\hat{b}_j / se_j\right)^2.
$$ {#eq-lr}

*Biological rationale:* Using $\mathbf{G}_u$ as the kinship correction
controls for population structure and cryptic relatedness. The $LR_j$
therefore measures the association of SNP $j$ *above and beyond* the
genomic background — not simply co-inheritance within families.

## Step 2 — Smooth the LRs with a Moving Average

$$
\overline{LR}_j(s) = \frac{1}{s} \sum_{\mathrm{window}} LR_k.
$$ {#eq-lr-smooth}

*Biological rationale:* A single SNP rarely sits exactly on a causal
variant; the true signal is spread across an LD block. Averaging $LR$
over $s$ neighbouring SNPs mimics the implicit model averaging of
Bayesian methods — SNPs in LD with the QTL collectively absorb its
signal. Window size $s$ is trait-dependent: traits with few large
QTLs converge with small $s$ (5–11 SNPs); highly polygenic traits
need larger $s$ (up to 81) to stabilise noisy per-SNP signals.

## Step 3 — Compute the Per-SNP Posterior Probability

$$
\overline{PP}_j
= \frac{\pi\,\exp(\overline{LR}_j)}
       {\pi\,\exp(\overline{LR}_j) + (1-\pi)},
\qquad \pi = 0.001.
$$ {#eq-pp}

*Biological rationale:* $\pi = 0.001$ encodes the prior belief that
roughly 0.1 % of SNPs on a standard chip sit close enough to a causal
variant to have a substantial effect — consistent with BayesC/BayesR
sparsity assumptions. The formula is exact Bayes: the likelihood ratio
$\exp(\overline{LR}_j)$ updates the prior odds $\pi/(1-\pi)$ to
posterior odds.

## Step 4 — Build the Weighted GRM

$$
\mathbf{G}_D
= \frac{\mathbf{W}\,\mathbf{D}\,\mathbf{W}^\top}
       {\sum_{j=1}^{p} 2p_j(1-p_j)\,D_{jj}},
\qquad D_{jj} = \overline{PP}_j.
$$ {#eq-grm-weighted}

::: {.callout-warning}
**Inflation risk and the min_weight floor.**
Because $\overline{PP}_j$ is computed from the *same* training data
used to fit the BLUP, there is mild information leakage: SNPs that
happen to correlate with the phenotype by chance get upweighted,
slightly inflating GEBVs. Meuwissen et al. (2024) report regression
coefficients of observed-on-predicted of 0.93–0.96 for dairy yield
traits — small but consistent. `masreml::gwablup()` imposes a
`min_weight` floor (default `1e-4`) for two reasons: (1) it prevents
any $D_{jj}$ from collapsing to zero, keeping $\mathbf{G}_D$
well-conditioned; (2) it limits the maximum upweighting of any single
SNP, partially mitigating inflation.
:::

## Step 5 — Solve the BLUP MME with $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{G}_D$

No new equations — this is the same MME solved in every other method.
The power of the unified framework: swapping **K** changes the biology
captured by the model without changing the solver.

::: {.callout-note}
**GWABLUP degrades gracefully for polygenic traits.**
When no genome-wide significant peaks exist, $\overline{LR}_j \approx 0$
for all SNPs, so $\overline{PP}_j \approx \pi$ everywhere. The
diagonal **D** becomes nearly constant and
$\mathbf{G}_D \approx \mathbf{G}_u$. GWABLUP collapses to standard
GBLUP, so there is no downside to always running it alongside GBLUP
on a new dataset.
:::

## See it in Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(masreml)

d <- load_data("large")
y <- d$pheno$y_cont_qtl_snp
names(y) <- d$pheno$id
X_fixed <- stats::model.matrix(~ sex, data = d$pheno)

# Fit a baseline GBLUP first — run_gwas() needs its variance components
fit_gblup <- masreml(
  y       = y,
  X       = X_fixed,
  markers = list(snp_add = d$snp),
  trait   = "continuous"
)

# Steps 1–3: EMMAX GWAS → LR smoothing → posterior probabilities
# pi = 0.001: prior probability that a SNP has a substantial effect
gwas <- run_gwas(
  markers     = list(snp_add = d$snp),
  y           = y,
  masreml_fit = fit_gblup,
  X           = X_fixed,
  pi          = 0.001,
  window      = 5L
)

# Steps 4–5: weighted G_D → BLUP solve
# min_weight = 1e-4: floor on D_jj to keep G_D well-conditioned
fit_gwa <- gwablup(
  y           = y,
  markers     = list(snp_add = d$snp),
  gwas_result = gwas,
  X           = X_fixed,
  min_weight  = 1e-4
)
summary(fit_gwa)
```
